article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 60% Indica / 40% Sativa
Genetics: Mimosa × Orange Punch
Breeder: Barney’s Farm
THC Content: 24–30%
CBD Content: Approximately 0.8%
Terpene Profile: Limonene , myrcene , beta-caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Tangerine, tropical lemon, sweet orange,
Flowering Time (Indoor): 65–70 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: October
Indoor Yield: 700–800 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: Up to 2,000 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Mimosa Evo takes a cannabis strain already famous for tasting like a citrus cocktail and turns nearly every characteristic upward. More fruit, larger plants, heavier flowers, deeper resin coverage, and considerably greater production are all part of Barney’s Farm’s interpretation of the original Mimosa genetics. The cultivar combines a selected Mimosa line with Orange Punch, creating flower that can smell like freshly peeled tangerines, tropical lemon, berry punch, and citrus candy before subtler earthy and spicy notes become apparent.

Despite being classified by the breeder as 60% indica, its personality does not follow the stereotype of a sleepy indica. The first stages of the high are typically cheerful, buoyant, and mentally active, while relaxation becomes more noticeable later. Barney’s Farm currently lists THC potential as high as 32%, an unusually strong figure for weed with such an approachable fruit-driven aroma. Its cultivation numbers are equally ambitious, with indoor production potentially reaching 700–800 g/m² and outdoor plants capable of growing beyond two meters.
Genetics and Lineage

The breeder-confirmed genetics of Mimosa Evo are Mimosa × Orange Punch. Barney’s Farm developed the strain using an Emerald Triangle Mimosa selection descended from the cultivar originally bred by Symbiotic Genetics , then crossed it with the company’s Orange Punch. The original Mimosa is itself Clementine × Purple Punch , which means the broader family combines vigorous citrus-heavy genetics with the darker fruit, resin, and physical influence of Purple Punch. Orange Punch intensifies the citrus side rather than attempting to replace it.

Clementine contributes much of the bright mandarin and tropical character associated with Mimosa, along with an energetic cerebral quality. Purple Punch provides berry sweetness, dense flowers, color potential, and a more relaxing physical component. Barney’s Orange Punch then pushes the family further toward orange peel, fruit punch, sweetness, and productive plant structure. The result is not merely a stronger version of Mimosa but a deliberate extension of its citrus profile into a larger, more indica-influenced plant.

Barney’s Farm calls the cultivar an evolution of the original Mimosa, which explains the “Evo” designation. This is also distinct from the company’s later Mimosa x Orange Punch strain, which was made by crossing Mimosa Evo back to Orange Punch again. That newer cultivar is therefore not genetically identical to Mimosa Evo despite the confusingly similar names.
Effects and Experience

The first part of the experience tends to feel considerably more energetic than the 60% indica classification suggests. Mood can rise rapidly, everyday activities may become more interesting, and conversation often takes on an easygoing, enthusiastic rhythm. Creative tasks, music, outdoor activities, and casual social situations can fit especially well with moderate consumption. Barney’s Farm characterizes the effect as happy, uplifting, and euphoric, while describing the cerebral sensation as light or “floaty.”

Physical relaxation usually becomes more apparent as the high matures. Rather than abruptly replacing the mental stimulation, the body effect tends to soften it. Muscles loosen, urgency fades, and the experience gradually becomes calmer while retaining some of its upbeat character. That progression gives this cultivar more versatility than marijuana that immediately produces either racing stimulation or heavy sedation.

Potency changes the equation dramatically. Earlier Barney’s Farm material placed THC mostly around 25–30%, while current breeder pages cite potential up to approximately 30–32%. At those concentrations, inexperienced consumers should use restraint. Too much can turn a cheerful cerebral buzz into dizziness, racing thoughts, anxiety, dry mouth, or significant impairment. The fruity flavor can make repeated inhalations deceptively easy, so allowing the first dose time to develop is sensible.
Medical Benefits

Medical marijuana consumers may appreciate Mimosa Evo when they prefer an uplifting cultivar that still develops meaningful physical relaxation. Smaller amounts may be attractive during periods of everyday stress, low mood, or mental fatigue because the initial experience generally feels brighter rather than sedating. The later body component can be more useful when relaxation becomes the priority.

Its daytime potential depends heavily on dosage. A modest amount may remain socially functional for an experienced consumer, whereas a larger serving of flower approaching 30% THC can become far more intoxicating. Anyone particularly sensitive to stimulating cannabis may also find the early cerebral component uncomfortable despite the strain’s eventual relaxing finish.

Mimosa Evo has not been clinically proven to treat depression, anxiety, pain, fatigue, or another medical condition. Cannabis effects vary according to dose, tolerance, cannabinoid chemistry, medications, physiology, and consumption method. Medical users should therefore evaluate the actual laboratory results of the product they are consuming rather than assuming that every harvest carrying the same strain name will behave identically.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Citrus dominates virtually every stage of the sensory experience. Barney’s Farm describes tropical lemon, orange, citrus, berries, fruit punch, and tangerine among the defining characteristics. Fresh flowers can smell like orange peel being twisted over a glass, releasing sweet citrus oil before berry and tropical-fruit aromas fill out the background. Some phenotypes bring more lemon sharpness, while others lean toward mandarin, grapefruit, or sugary orange candy.

Commonly reported terpene profiles place limonene near the center of the cultivar, with myrcene and beta-caryophyllene also associated with Mimosa Evo flower. Exact terpene dominance varies with phenotype and cultivation. Limonene complements the orange and lemon profile, myrcene can add ripe fruit and earthy depth, and caryophyllene contributes subtle peppery spice that becomes easier to notice once the flower is broken apart.

The flavor typically begins sweeter than it finishes. Orange, tangerine, tropical fruit, and berry arrive through the inhale, followed by citrus zest and a mild earthy or peppery quality on the exhale. Proper drying and curing matter considerably with this weed because volatile citrus terpenes are among the first aromatic components to suffer when flower is dried too quickly or stored poorly.
Growing Information

Mimosa Evo is capable of becoming a large and highly productive cannabis plant. Barney’s Farm currently lists indoor height at approximately 100–120 cm, with potential yields around 700–800 g/m². Outdoors, plants can reach roughly 180–220 cm and potentially produce as much as 2,000 grams per plant under exceptional conditions. Those are breeder potential figures rather than guaranteed harvests, but they demonstrate the production-oriented nature of the genetics.

Indoor flowering generally requires 65–70 days. The plant responds well to training because controlling its canopy allows more flowering sites to receive strong light. Topping, low-stress training, and trellising can help distribute vigorous growth horizontally, while selective removal of weak interior branches improves airflow and directs resources toward stronger colas. Dense, resin-heavy flowers make humidity management increasingly important near harvest.

Outdoor cultivation is where its size becomes most obvious. Barney’s Farm places harvest during October, currently specifying approximately the third to fourth week, although older material sometimes referenced an earlier October finish. Warm conditions, unrestricted roots, direct sunlight, and enough seasonal time allow plants to approach their full potential. Growers in rainy autumn climates should monitor dense flowers carefully as maturity approaches.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Mimosa Evo?
Mimosa Evo is Mimosa × Orange Punch, bred by Barney’s Farm. The Mimosa parent traces to the famous Clementine × Purple Punch cultivar originally created by Symbiotic Genetics.
Is Mimosa Evo indica or sativa?

Barney’s Farm classifies the strain as 60% indica and 40% sativa. Despite the indica majority, its early effects are often energetic, euphoric, and mentally uplifting before stronger relaxation develops.
How strong is Mimosa Evo?

It is a high-potency strain. Barney’s Farm historically listed roughly 25–30% THC potential and now advertises selected plants capable of reaching approximately 32%. Actual potency varies with phenotype and cultivation.
What does Mimosa Evo taste like?

Tangerine, orange, tropical lemon, berry, and fruit punch dominate the flavor. Depending on the phenotype, the citrus can resemble fresh orange peel, grapefruit, mandarin candy, or sweet tropical fruit.
How long does Mimosa Evo take to flower?
Indoor flowering takes approximately 65–70 days. Outdoors, Barney’s Farm currently places harvest during the third to fourth week of October in the Northern Hemisphere.
Final Thoughts on Mimosa Evo

Mimosa Evo succeeds because Barney’s Farm amplified the best-known qualities of Mimosa without turning it into an entirely different style of weed. The original Clementine and Purple Punch background supplies citrus, berries, resin, and a lively cerebral experience, while Orange Punch intensifies the fruit and contributes the structure needed for significantly larger harvests. The result remains recognizably Mimosa, but louder, heavier, and more productive.

The cultivation specifications are particularly impressive: a 65–70-day flowering period, indoor yields potentially reaching 700–800 g/m², outdoor plants exceeding two meters, and breeder-reported THC potential around 30% or higher. Yet potency and yield are only part of the attraction. Mimosa Evo’s enduring appeal lies in the contrast between its tropical orange aroma and its evolving high—bright and energetic at first, increasingly relaxed afterward. For cannabis enthusiasts who enjoy citrus-heavy marijuana but want more potency, resin, and production than traditional Mimosa typically offers, Mimosa Evo represents a carefully engineered extension of an already celebrated genetic family.
